opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most underrated problems in evaluation right now. Most of our benchmarks are basically multiple-choice or exact-match accuracy, and that setup rewards guessing. If the model says "I don't know," it gets zero. If it guesses, it has some chance of being right. So you train models, directly or indirectly, to bluff. Then we act surprised when they hallucinate.

What I'd like to see is evaluation that treats abstention as a real outcome. Instead of a binary right or wrong, you'd have three cases: correct, wrong, and "I don't know." Then you penalize confident wrong answers more than abstentions. It's a bit like those exams where wrong answers cost you points, so you only answer when you're fairly sure. That changes the incentives a lot.

You also want to look at calibration, not just accuracy. If a model says it's 90% confident, is it right about 90% of the time? You can measure that, and you can draw curves: how accuracy improves as you let the model abstain on more questions. A good model should get much more accurate as it declines the questions it's unsure about. A badly calibrated one won't improve much, because its uncertainty doesn't track its errors.

The tricky part is that you don't want to over-reward refusing. Otherwise the model learns that saying "I don't know" is always safe, and it becomes useless. So the right metric depends on the use case. In a medical or legal setting, a wrong answer is very costly, so abstaining should score well. In a brainstorming or creative setting, you'd rather it try. Ideally the benchmark makes that cost explicit, instead of assuming every error costs the same.

And the last piece is that "I don't know" shouldn't be the end of the conversation. In agentic settings, the best response is often "I'm not sure, let me check," and then it uses a tool or searches. So I think evaluations should increasingly reward a model that knows the limits of its knowledge and does something useful about them, not just one that memorized the most facts.

r001.rationale: The response proposes treating abstention as a distinct evaluation outcome, listing “correct, wrong, and ‘I don't know’” after noting that common benchmarks use multiple choice or exact match.

r002.rationale: It discusses abstention rates and accuracy as questions are declined, but does not say that models with identical overall accuracy can differ in how often they abstain.

r003.rationale: It favors abstention in high-cost settings, but does not express the specified preference between models that are equally accurate on the questions they answer.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So this is something I care about a lot, because I think the way we evaluate models today actively punishes honesty.

Think about how most benchmarks work. You have a question, you have a gold answer, and you score the model on whether it matches. If the model says "I don't know," that counts as a zero, exactly the same as a confidently wrong answer. So from the model's perspective, during training, there is never any reason to abstain. If you have a one percent chance of being right by guessing, guessing is strictly better than saying you don't know. We are literally optimizing for hallucination and then complaining that models hallucinate.

What I would like is for evaluations to make abstention a first-class outcome with its own reward structure. The simplest version is something like negative marking, the way some exams do it. A correct answer gets a point, an "I don't know" gets zero, and a wrong answer gets a negative score. Suddenly the optimal policy changes. The model should only answer when its confidence is above some threshold, and that threshold is set by the penalty. You can even vary the penalty across the benchmark to probe how well-calibrated the model is at different risk levels.

The second thing is that we should separate two capabilities that we currently blend together. One is knowledge: does the model actually know the answer? The other is self-knowledge: does the model know whether it knows? Those are different skills, and the second one is arguably more important for deployment. A model that knows less but knows exactly where its boundaries are is much safer to put in front of users than a model that knows a bit more but will confidently make things up at the edges. Right now we have almost no benchmarks that measure the second thing in isolation.

There is a subtlety, which is that you don't want to over-reward abstention either. A model that says "I don't know" to everything is useless, and a model that abstains on easy questions is being lazy, not humble. So the evaluation has to check that the abstentions are concentrated where the model would actually have been wrong. That is basically a calibration measurement, and I think the metric we should be reporting is something like: of the questions the model refused, what fraction would it have gotten wrong? And of the ones it answered, what was the accuracy? Those two numbers together tell you far more than a single aggregate score.

And honestly, this matters for how we train, not just how we report. When we did post-training on Llama, one of the things we found is that if you reward the model for saying it doesn't know on questions it genuinely cannot answer, and you build that data carefully by checking what the model actually knows versus what it is guessing, hallucination goes down a lot without hurting helpfulness much. But that only works if the people building the benchmarks give you credit for it. Otherwise every team is incentivized to ship the model that guesses, because that is the one that tops the leaderboard.

So my short answer is: stop treating "I don't know" as a failure. Treat it as a measurable, rewardable behavior, score it against the counterfactual, and report calibration alongside accuracy. If we do that, I think the models will follow very quickly, because they will simply be optimizing for what we are actually measuring.

r001.rationale: The response proposes making abstention a rewarded evaluation outcome, but does not specify adding an “I don't know” choice to multiple-choice evaluations.

r002.rationale: It recommends reporting abstention and answer accuracy separately, but does not state that models with identical overall accuracy can differ in how often they abstain.

r003.rationale: It favors a model that knows its limits in general, but does not express this preference for the stated case where both models get the same proportion of all questions correct.

astra-6.text:
I’d like evaluations to reward a model for knowing when it doesn’t know. If you only measure accuracy and every question requires an answer, you’re encouraging the model to guess. A correct guess gets rewarded, while an honest “I don’t know” gets treated as a failure.

So I would look at accuracy together with how often the model chooses to answer. If it answers fewer questions, are those answers more reliable? Can it distinguish between something it knows, something it’s uncertain about, and something it needs more information to answer?

Of course, a model that always says “I don’t know” isn’t useful either. The goal is to reward useful answers and appropriate uncertainty together. That’s much closer to what we actually want when we use these systems.

r001.rationale: The response discusses rewarding appropriate uncertainty, but it does not propose an explicit “I don't know” option in multiple-choice evaluations.

r002.rationale: It recommends considering accuracy alongside answer frequency, but does not state that models with identical overall accuracy can differ in abstention frequency.

r003.rationale: It favors useful answers and appropriate uncertainty together, but does not express the specified preference when both models get the same proportion of all questions correct.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d like evaluations to reward a model for saying “I don’t know” when it genuinely doesn’t have enough information. If the only thing you measure is whether the answer is correct, and a wrong answer gets the same score as abstaining, you’re encouraging the model to guess.

But you also don’t want a model that says “I don’t know” to everything. So you need to measure both: how often it answers, and how reliable it is when it does answer. Can it distinguish a question it can solve from one where it’s missing information? For me, that’s part of the capability we should evaluate.

r001.rationale: It supports rewarding “I don’t know,” but does not propose adding that as an explicit option in multiple-choice evaluations.

r002.rationale: It says to measure answer frequency and reliability, but does not state that equal overall accuracy can hide differences in abstention rates.

r003.rationale: It does not express a preference between models that answer the same proportion correctly but abstain at different rates.
